sources.title: JOIN
sources.reviewedEvidence: Search-result title and snippet confirmed 2026-09-23; page body not fetched in this build (documentation host blocked by the sandbox egress proxy). Passage relied on, as previously read: The JOIN clause combines the rows of the left table reference with the right table reference based on join criteria; an INNER join returns the rows that have matching values in both table references and is the default join type; a LEFT join returns all values from the left table reference and the matched values from the right, or appends NULL if there is no match; join criteria are given with ON boolean_expression or USING (column list).
sources.caveat: Standard SQL semantics; row multiplication is a property of matching pairs, not of Databricks.

sources.title: Databricks SDK for Python v0.141.0: service/serving.py
sources.reviewedEvidence: Read in this build on 2026-09-23: fetched from the v0.141.0 tag via raw.githubusercontent.com; its SHA-256 (c9931801e5d9802b...) equals serving.py in the databricks-sdk 0.141.0 wheel downloaded from PyPI (wheel SHA-256 053ddd3702b5ed99..., uploaded 2026-09-23). Passages relied on: ServingEndpointsAPI says endpoints expose models as scalable REST endpoints on serverless compute fully managed by Databricks that do not appear in the customer's cloud account, and an endpoint holds at most ten served entities with traffic routes; the ServingEndpoint.ai_gateway field and put_ai_gateway note that external model, provisioned throughput and pay-per-token endpoints are fully supported while agent endpoints currently only support inference tables; AiGatewayConfig holds fallback_config, guardrails, inference_table_config, rate_limits and usage_tracking_config; a rate limit counts calls or tokens per minute keyed by endpoint (the default), user, user group or service principal; guardrails carry a safety flag, a PII behavior of BLOCK, MASK or NONE, invalid keywords and valid topics; usage tracking uses system tables to monitor operational usage on endpoints and their associated costs; a query's client_request_id is recorded in the inference table and the usage tracking table; ExternalModel providers are ai21labs, anthropic, amazon-bedrock, cohere, databricks-model-serving, google-cloud-vertex-ai, openai, palm and custom; provisioned-throughput served entities take provisioned_model_units and burst_scaling_enabled (on by default); endpoint permission levels are CAN_MANAGE, CAN_QUERY and CAN_VIEW; the older put method for rate limits is deprecated in favour of AI Gateway.
sources.caveat: A client field proves an API shape, not that a feature is enabled for a cloud, region, workspace or endpoint type; docstrings can lag or lead the product documentation.

sources.title: Databricks SDK for Python v0.141.0: service/catalog.py (AiGatewayAPI)
sources.reviewedEvidence: Read in this build on 2026-09-23 from the v0.141.0 tag; SHA-256 (ce451408065ee52e...) equals catalog.py in the PyPI wheel. Passages relied on: AiGatewayAPI governs AI workloads in Unity Catalog through model services (governed access to foundation models and external LLMs), model provider services (governed resources for external model providers) and MCP services (governed Model Context Protocol servers); a ModelService is a governed AI Gateway endpoint in Unity Catalog that routes inference requests to destinations of type pay-per-token, provisioned-throughput or external foundation model and applies centralized access control, rate limits and auditing; its configuration holds routing with fallback, rate limits and an inference table; creating one requires CREATE_SERVICE and USE_SCHEMA on the parent schema, USE_CATALOG on its catalog and EXECUTE on each referenced model or model provider service, and a provisioned-throughput destination also requires CAN_MANAGE on its Model Serving endpoint.
sources.caveat: A second surface named AI Gateway, separate from a serving endpoint's ai_gateway settings; release stage and regional availability are not stated in the client.

sources.title: Spark 4.0.4 SQL reference: NULL semantics
sources.reviewedEvidence: Search-result title and snippet confirmed 2026-09-23; page body not fetched in this build (documentation host blocked by the sandbox egress proxy). sources.title: Databricks SQL: TIMEZONE configuration parameter
sources.reviewedEvidence: Search-result title and snippet confirmed 2026-09-23; page body not fetched in this build (documentation host blocked by the sandbox egress proxy). Passage relied on, as previously read: the TIMEZONE parameter controls the local time zone used for timestamp operations in a session, can be set with SET at the session level or globally for a SQL warehouse, and the system default is UTC; an alternative way to set the session time zone is the SET TIME ZONE statement; a zone is a region ID of the form area/city such as America/Los_Angeles, an offset such as -08 or +01:00, or UTC as an alias for +00:00.

sources.title: Databricks: Dates and timestamps (Spark 3.x migration archive)
sources.reviewedEvidence: Search-result title and snippet confirmed 2026-09-23; page body not fetched in this build (documentation host blocked by the sandbox egress proxy). Passage relied on, as previously read: Spark delegates the mapping between local timestamps and instants to the Java standard library and the IANA time zone database; in a gap, where clocks jump forward, there is no valid offset and, for a typical one-hour change, Spark moves the timestamp to the next valid timestamp in summer time; in an overlap, where clocks jump backward, a local timestamp such as 2019-11-03 01:30:00 America/Los_Angeles maps to two offsets and Databricks Runtime 7.0 takes the earlier one, typically corresponding to summer time.
sources.caveat: An archive page for Spark 3.x; both the gap and the overlap behaviour were re-observed on local Spark 4.0.4 in Lab L12 and are recorded as observed, not promised.

sources.title: ORDER BY Clause (Spark SQL)
sources.reviewedEvidence: Search-result title and snippet confirmed 2026-09-23; page body not fetched in this build (documentation host blocked by the sandbox egress proxy). sources.caveat: Default NULL placement is Spark's rule; other engines differ, so a report that depends on it writes NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST.

sources.title: ANSI Compliance (Spark SQL)

sources.caveat: Describes open-source Spark defaults; a Databricks runtime or warehouse documents its own ANSI setting, so check it on the target.

sources.title: Configure authorization in a Databricks app
sources.reviewedEvidence: Not confirmed by search for this record: the build session's web-search budget was exhausted (200 of 200 searches) before this module was written on 2026-09-23, so the title and URL are as supplied in the build's source list and as previously read; page body not fetched in this build (documentation host blocked by the sandbox egress proxy). Passage relied on, as previously read: each Databricks app has a dedicated service principal that is unique to the app and cannot be reused by another app; Databricks injects its OAuth credentials into the app environment as DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID and DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET; with app authorization, calls are evaluated against that principal's permissions whoever the signed-in user is; with user authorization, the platform forwards the user's access token in the X-Forwarded-Access-Token header, calls made with it are evaluated with the user's own permissions, and the app declares scopes such as sql that restrict what it can do on the user's behalf, with access outside approved scopes blocked even when the user holds broader permissions.
sources.caveat: User authorization has carried a Public Preview label and may need to be enabled for the workspace; scope names and the APIs each scope covers must be read from the current page before an app is designed around them. No app was configured.

sources.title: Table deletes, updates, and merges
sources.reviewedEvidence: Page source read in full on 2026-09-23 from raw.githubusercontent.com at tag v4.0.0 of the delta-io/delta repository (the Markdown behind the docs.delta.io page; the rendered site is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy and was not fetched). Passages relied on: delete removes data from the latest version but not from physical storage until old versions are vacuumed; MERGE supports inserts, updates and deletes; whenMatched clauses may update or delete, whenNotMatched clauses may only insert, and whenNotMatchedBySource clauses may update or delete target rows that no source row matches and cannot reference source columns; clauses of one kind are evaluated in order and all but the last need a condition; a target row that no clause selects is left unchanged; a merge can fail when multiple source rows match and attempt to update the same target row, and the source should be preprocessed to keep one change per key; updateAll and insertAll ignore extra source columns unless automatic schema evolution is enabled; NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE is available in the APIs from Delta 2.3 and in SQL from 2.4, and an optional condition is recommended. The delta-spark 4.0.0 jar's own multiple-match error message links to this page.
sources.caveat: Open-source semantics at one release. Databricks runs its own Delta implementation, and runtime-specific details such as which conditions count toward a duplicate match can differ; check the platform's MERGE reference for the runtime in use.

sources.title: delta.tables Python API: DeltaMergeBuilder
sources.reviewedEvidence: Read locally on 2026-09-23 in the installed delta-spark 4.0.0 package source (delta/tables.py from the published wheel, delta_spark-4.0.0.dist-info). Passages relied on: DeltaMergeBuilder.withSchemaEvolution() is marked @since(3.2) and documented as enabling schema evolution for the merge operation, so the target schema is updated from the source DataFrame's schema. Executed in this review on local Apache Spark 4.0.4 with delta-spark 4.0.0 and spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled unset: a MERGE with whenMatchedUpdateAll, whenNotMatchedInsertAll and withSchemaEvolution added the source's extra column; the same MERGE without it ignored the column; the SQL statement MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION INTO parsed and merged the rows but added no column.
sources.caveat: The API source can run ahead of the documentation pages; this module's docs source still names only the session setting for MERGE schema evolution. Databricks documents its own MERGE schema evolution syntax per runtime.

sources.title: Table batch reads and writes
sources.reviewedEvidence: Page source read in full on 2026-09-23 from raw.githubusercontent.com at tag v4.0.0 of the delta-io/delta repository (the Markdown behind the docs.delta.io page; the rendered site is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy and was not fetched). Passages relied on: writes are validated against the table schema: every DataFrame column must exist in the table and data types must match, otherwise an exception is raised, and table columns missing from the DataFrame are written as null; columns can be added explicitly with ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMNS or automatically with the mergeSchema write option or the spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled session setting, the write option taking precedence and added columns being appended at the end; overwriteSchema replaces the schema on an overwrite; streams that read a table terminate when its schema is updated; time travel needs both the log and the data files of a version; data files are deleted only by VACUUM; delta.logRetentionDuration defaults to 30 days and delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration to 7 days; log cleanup at checkpoints can leave a version inside the retention window unreadable because every log entry since the previous checkpoint is needed.
sources.caveat: Open-source Delta 4.0.0 behaviour; streaming behaviour and platform defaults differ by engine and release.

sources.title: Change data feed
sources.reviewedEvidence: Page source read in full on 2026-09-23 from raw.githubusercontent.com at tag v4.0.0 of the delta-io/delta repository (the Markdown behind the docs.delta.io page; the rendered site is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy and was not fetched). Passages relied on: the change data feed is not enabled by default and is enabled per table with delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true; only changes made after enabling are recorded and past changes are not captured; after enabling, Delta 1.2.1 or below can no longer write the table; UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE changes are stored under _change_data, while insert-only operations can be computed from the log; change files follow the table's retention and VACUUM deletes them; batch reads take inclusive start and end versions or timestamps and fail for versions before the feed was enabled; the metadata columns are _change_type (insert, update_preimage, update_postimage, delete), _commit_version and _commit_timestamp; a stream without a starting version first returns the latest snapshot as inserts.
sources.caveat: Open-source change data feed as of Delta 4.0.0. Databricks documents an additional automatic mode for eligible Unity Catalog tables; verify which mode a table uses.

sources.title: Table utility commands
sources.reviewedEvidence: Page source read in full on 2026-09-23 from raw.githubusercontent.com at tag v4.0.0 of the delta-io/delta repository (the Markdown behind the docs.delta.io page; the rendered site is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy and was not fetched). Passages relied on: vacuum removes files that are no longer referenced by a Delta table and are older than the retention threshold; it is not triggered automatically and the default threshold is 7 days; it deletes only data files, not log files; the ability to time travel to a version older than the retention is lost after vacuum; VACUUM ... DRY RUN lists the files to be deleted; LITE mode (Delta 3.3 and above) uses the transaction log instead of listing the directory and raises DELTA_CANNOT_VACUUM_LITE when the log has been pruned; the documentation recommends a retention of at least 7 days because concurrent readers or writers may still use old snapshots and uncommitted files, and removing active files can make readers fail or corrupt the table; a safety check exists to prevent a dangerous VACUUM; DESCRIBE HISTORY reports MERGE metrics such as numSourceRows, numTargetRowsInserted, numTargetRowsUpdated and numTargetRowsDeleted, and OPTIMIZE metrics such as numAddedFiles and numRemovedFiles.
sources.caveat: Open-source VACUUM semantics. The retention a shared table keeps is a decision for its owners and readers, never a default to shorten for convenience.

sources.title: Optimizations
sources.reviewedEvidence: Page source read in full on 2026-09-23 from raw.githubusercontent.com at tag v4.0.0 of the delta-io/delta repository (the Markdown behind the docs.delta.io page; the rendered site is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy and was not fetched). Passages relied on: compaction (bin-packing) coalesces small files into larger ones, is idempotent, and makes no data-related change, so a read before and after returns the same results; readers use snapshot isolation and are not interrupted when OPTIMIZE removes files from the log; OPTIMIZE accepts a partition predicate; Z-ordering colocates related values, is not idempotent and re-clusters all files of a partition on every run; auto compaction (Delta 3.1 and above) runs synchronously after a successful write; optimized writes (Delta 3.1 and above) are disabled by default; data-skipping statistics are collected on the leading columns set by delta.dataSkippingNumIndexedCols.
sources.caveat: Open-source defaults (for example optimized writes disabled) may differ from a managed platform's defaults; check the engine in use before assuming a behaviour.

sources.title: Use liquid clustering for Delta tables
sources.reviewedEvidence: Page source read in full on 2026-09-23 from raw.githubusercontent.com at tag v4.0.0 of the delta-io/delta repository (the Markdown behind the docs.delta.io page; the rendered site is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy and was not fetched). Passages relied on: liquid clustering (Delta 3.1 and above) is enabled with CLUSTER BY at creation and, from Delta 3.3, on an existing unpartitioned table; it is not compatible with partitioning or ZORDER; OPTIMIZE clusters data incrementally and OPTIMIZE FULL (3.3 and above) reclusters all records; clustering columns can be changed with ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY without rewriting existing data, or turned off with NONE; tables created with clustering have the Clustering and DomainMetadata writer features, writer version 7 and reader version 1, and protocol versions cannot be downgraded; up to 4 clustering columns are allowed, each with collected statistics; DESCRIBE DETAIL shows the clustering columns.
sources.caveat: Open-source liquid clustering as of Delta 4.0.0; automatic key selection is a Databricks capability that this page does not cover.

sources.title: How does Delta Lake manage feature compatibility?
sources.reviewedEvidence: Page source read in full on 2026-09-23 from raw.githubusercontent.com at tag v4.0.0 of the delta-io/delta repository (the Markdown behind the docs.delta.io page; the rendered site is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy and was not fetched). Passages relied on: features are backward compatible, but enabling some breaks forward compatibility, so every workload that references an upgraded table must use a compliant version; a table protocol has a read side and a write side, and a client that does not understand a listed feature cannot read or write the table; CHECK constraints and the change data feed only upgrade the write protocol, while column mapping and deletion vectors also upgrade the read protocol; table features (Delta 2.3.0 and above) are granular flags that succeed protocol versions; the change data feed maps to writer version 4 and reader version 1 in the legacy scheme; protocol version upgrades are irreversible and can break existing readers, writers or both.
sources.caveat: Feature lists and minimum versions change with releases; compare every client against the table's DESCRIBE DETAIL output before enabling a feature.

sources.title: What are deletion vectors?
sources.reviewedEvidence: Page source read in full on 2026-09-23 from raw.githubusercontent.com at tag v4.0.0 of the delta-io/delta repository (the Markdown behind the docs.delta.io page; the rendered site is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy and was not fetched). Passages relied on: by default, deleting a single row rewrites the entire Parquet file that contains it; with deletion vectors enabled, some operations mark rows as removed without rewriting the file and readers apply the marks; enabling them upgrades the table protocol, so clients without support cannot read the table; modified data can remain in old files until they are rewritten and vacuumed, and REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE) rewrites files to purge soft-deleted rows.
sources.caveat: Deletion vectors are optional in open-source Delta 4.0.0 and the lab's table does not use them; platform defaults can differ, so read DESCRIBE DETAIL rather than assume.

sources.title: databricks-sdk 0.141.0 (Databricks SDK for Python)
sources.reviewedEvidence: Read in this session: the wheel databricks_sdk-0.141.0-py3-none-any.whl was downloaded from PyPI on 2026-09-23, its SHA-256 matched the index (053ddd3702b5ed99e01951915fc3421565fc72f82f41623d51e13a0209ba2b79), and these docstrings were read locally. ClustersAPI: all-purpose clusters are used to analyze data collaboratively in interactive notebooks and can be terminated and restarted manually and shared; job clusters run automated jobs; Databricks maps node instance types to compute units known as DBUs. autotermination_minutes: a cluster inactive for that many minutes terminates, and a cluster with the field unset is not terminated automatically. custom_tags: Databricks tags all cluster resources, such as AWS instances and EBS volumes, with them in addition to default tags. InstancePoolsAPI: pools keep idle, ready-to-use instances to reduce cluster start and autoscaling times; Databricks does not charge DBUs while instances are idle in the pool, and instance provider billing does apply. SQL warehouses: auto_stop_mins is the idle time before a warehouse stops, 0 meaning no autostop and 120 minutes the default; cluster_size lets larger queries run, while concurrent queries are tuned with max_num_clusters; min_num_clusters keeps clusters running, which may reduce cold start time; tags are applied to all resources such as AWS instances and EBS volumes. QueryMetrics: provisioning_queue_start_timestamp marks waiting for a cluster to be provisioned and overloading_queue_start_timestamp marks waiting while the warehouse is at max load, beside compilation and execution times. Jobs: new_cluster describes a cluster created for each run; running on an existing cluster may need manual restarts, so new clusters are suggested for reliability; jobs and runs record the usage policy used for cost attribution. TerminationReasonCode includes AWS_RESOURCE_QUOTA_EXCEEDED and AWS_INSUFFICIENT_INSTANCE_CAPACITY_FAILURE; NodeTypeFlexibility lists alternate node types used as fallbacks when the primary node type is unavailable during launch and upscale. ClusterPoliciesAPI: policies limit the attributes users can set, including limits on attributes that impact the hourly rate. Budgets: alert thresholds are measured as LIST_PRICE_DOLLARS_USD over a MONTH and trigger on CUMULATIVE_SPENDING_EXCEEDED, scoped shared or per user, with EMAIL_NOTIFICATION and BLOCK_USAGE action types; budget policies carry customer-defined custom tags.
sources.caveat: API reference text in a Beta SDK names fields, defaults and enumerations, not recommended settings; product behaviour is confirmed in the current documentation for the workspace's cloud and region.

sources.title: Cross-validation: evaluating estimator performance
sources.reviewedEvidence: Reused record: the URL, title and publisher are those the machine-learning foundations module reviewed on 2026-09-20; not re-confirmed by search in this build session, whose web-search budget was exhausted (200 of 200 searches) on 2026-09-23, and the page body was not fetched here (documentation host blocked by the sandbox egress proxy). Passage relied on, as previously read: time series observations are correlated with observations near them in time, so classical cross-validation that assumes independent samples, such as KFold and ShuffleSplit, would put unreasonably correlated observations in training and test sets; TimeSeriesSplit instead returns the first k folds as the training set and the (k+1)th as the test set, each successive training set a superset of the one before.
sources.caveat: A split strategy is only valid if it matches the decision's timing; no split guarantees deployed accuracy.

Passages relied on: a customer service account is added to the account console as an account admin and impersonated by listed principals; the Databricks Workspace Creator custom role lists permissions to create IAM roles and service accounts, read and set the project's IAM policy, enable services, read networks and subnetworks and set subnetwork IAM, read and create firewall rules, and read forwarding rules when PSC is used; account-level APIs are called by account owners and admins and authenticated only with Google-issued OIDC tokens; the example VPC is custom mode, its subnet enables Private Google Access, and a Cloud Router and Cloud NAT are created before the workspace for outbound traffic; pod and service ranges and gke_config are deprecated and no longer supported.
sources.caveat: A provider guide provided as-is, not the product documentation; its examples pin old provider versions and example regions and defer networking detail to the customer-managed VPC page.

sources.title: Databricks Terraform provider v1.133.0: Provisioning Databricks workspaces on GCP with Private Service Connect (guide)
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the provider's v1.133.0 tag (release dated 2026-09-21 in the provider changelog) through its raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; the mws_vpc_endpoint, mws_private_access_settings and mws_networks resource pages at the same tag were read with it, and all matched the module archive and the main branch. Passages relied on: back-end PSC (data plane to control plane) configures the network with two back-end VPC endpoints, one for the secure cluster connectivity relay and one for REST APIs; a front-end endpoint in a transit (bastion) VPC carries user connections to the web application, REST API and Databricks Connect API; a workspace must be created with private access settings to support any PSC scenario; a GCP VPC endpoint is registered with the project ID of the VPC network where the PSC connection resides, the PSC endpoint name and its region, and exports psc_connection_id and service_attachment_id; public_access_enabled defaults to false on AWS and true on GCP; ACCOUNT level admits endpoints registered in the account, ENDPOINT level only allowed_vpc_endpoint_ids; with public access enabled, IP access lists restrict public sources.
sources.caveat: The guide's workspace example still carries a gke_config block that the workspace resource page marks deprecated; its examples are shapes to read, not configurations to copy.

sources.title: Databricks Terraform provider v1.133.0: databricks_mws_workspaces and databricks_mws_networks resources
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the provider's v1.133.0 tag (release dated 2026-09-21 in the provider changelog) through its raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; the mws_networks page at the same tag was read with it; both matched the module archive and the main branch. Passages relied on: a serverless workspace is created with compute_mode SERVERLESS and a location and needs no prerequisite resources; cloud_resource_container.gcp.project_id is the project the workspace uses to instantiate cloud resources; by default Databricks creates a VPC in the GCP project for each workspace, a customer-managed VPC is recommended, and an existing workspace cannot be migrated to it; one customer-managed VPC can serve several workspaces but subnets cannot be reused by other workspaces or resources; gcp_workspace_sa has the form db-<workspace-id>@prod-gcp-<region>.iam.gserviceaccount.com; effective_compute_mode is SERVERLESS or HYBRID; on GCP the subnet is in the workspace region, its range allocates GCE cluster nodes, its netmask is between /29 and /9, and it needs outbound access to the public network through Cloud NAT or a similar customer-managed appliance; on AWS the network needs at least two subnets in different availability zones with netmasks between /17 and /25, plus security groups.
sources.caveat: Resource documentation describes API fields and examples; it is not a statement of regional availability, and some examples still show deprecated GKE fields.

sources.title: Databricks Terraform provider v1.133.0: Unity Catalog set up on Google Cloud (guide)
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the provider's v1.133.0 tag (release dated 2026-09-21 in the provider changelog) through its raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; the storage_credential, cluster and sql_global_config resource pages at the same tag were read with it; all matched the module archive and the main branch. Passages relied on: databricks_gcp_service_account creates a Databricks-managed GCP service account whose email is output only and is to be granted access to relevant buckets; the guide binds roles/storage.objectAdmin and roles/storage.legacyBucketReader on the bucket to that email; for file events it grants a custom role with Pub/Sub subscription and topic permissions and storage.buckets.update to that email at project level, and roles/pubsub.publisher to the project's Cloud Storage service account; external locations use gs:// URLs; one metastore per region; a cluster's gcp_attributes.google_service_account is the Google service account the cluster uses to authenticate for Cloud Storage and BigQuery; on AWS a storage credential's IAM role requires a trust policy.
sources.caveat: Provided as-is: the guide's code has inconsistent resource names and grants roles broader than read-only; take the mechanism from it and the minimum roles from the current Databricks page.

sources.title: Databricks Terraform provider v1.133.0: network connectivity configuration and network policy resources
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the provider's v1.133.0 tag (release dated 2026-09-21 in the provider changelog) through its raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; the mws_network_connectivity_config, mws_ncc_private_endpoint_rule and account_network_policy pages at the same tag were read with it and matched the module archive; on the main branch the first three were identical and the network policy page differed only by an added excluded_scopes field. Passages relied on: the NCC binding is available for AWS and Azure only and in Public Preview on AWS; NCC private endpoint rules are available on Azure and in Public Preview on AWS; NCC default rules document aws_stable_ip_rule and azure_service_endpoint_rule, and target rules document Azure and AWS private endpoint rules only; each account has a default network policy associated with workspaces that lack an assignment; policies allow internet destinations by DNS name and storage destinations whose types include GOOGLE_CLOUD_STORAGE, enforced or in dry run.
sources.caveat: Provider documentation can lag the product; a statement that a feature is AWS and Azure only is evidence for an unknown on Google Cloud, not proof of absence.

sources.title: Databricks Terraform provider v1.133.0: Provisioning Azure Databricks with Private Link, standard deployment (guide)
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the provider's v1.133.0 tag (release dated 2026-09-21 in the provider changelog) through its raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; it matched the module archive. Passages relied on: the standard deployment uses a transit virtual network and a data plane virtual network, with private endpoints for back-end connectivity, front-end connectivity and web authentication (browser_authentication); workspace subnets are delegated to Microsoft.Databricks/workspaces and associated with network security groups; the workspace is an azurerm_databricks_workspace resource in a resource group whose custom parameters name the virtual network and its public and private subnets.
sources.caveat: Contrast evidence only: the Azure module owns Azure answers, and this module never uses them to fill a Google Cloud cell.

sources.title: Databricks SDK for Python v0.141.0: service/provisioning.py (workspaces, networks, private access and keys)
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read for its Google Cloud classes on 2026-09-23 from the tagged raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; its SHA-256 matches the same file in the databricks-sdk 0.141.0 wheel published on PyPI that day, whose own digest matched PyPI's record. service/catalog.py at the same tag was read for the storage credential classes and also matched. Passages relied on: network_project_id is the GCP project for network resources, where the VPC and subnet reside; dataplane_relay and rest_api are the VPC endpoints a network uses for the secure cluster connectivity relay and the REST API; a workspace's location is the Google Cloud region of its data plane; storage modes are CUSTOMER_HOSTED and DEFAULT_STORAGE; the service account with access to a GCP KMS key exists within the Databricks control-plane project, and with manual set Databricks will not use OAuth to grant it access; public access can be disabled only with both front-end and back-end private connections; a Databricks GCP service account credential is a Databricks-created Google Cloud Storage service account identified by credential ID and email.
sources.caveat: API docstrings, some worded for AWS; they describe fields, not regional or tier availability.

sources.title: Databricks SDK for Python v0.141.0: service/settings.py (network connectivity configurations and network policies)
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read for its NCC and network policy classes on 2026-09-23 from the tagged raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; its SHA-256 matches the same file in the PyPI wheel for 0.141.0. Passages relied on: NCC private endpoint rules carry a gcp_endpoint with a target service attachment (example projects/my-gcp-project/regions/us-east4/serviceAttachments/my-service-attachment), selected Google API hostnames such as storage.googleapis.com, an option covering all Google APIs that support VPC Service Controls, and an output PSC endpoint URI; the rule's enabled flag is honoured only for first-party services such as AWS S3; network policy storage destinations include GOOGLE_CLOUD_STORAGE.
sources.caveat: A schema field shows what the API can describe; it does not show availability for an account, region or release stage.

sources.title: Databricks Security Reference Architecture templates: Google Cloud README
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the main branch through its raw URL (SHA-256 1347212b52f9...), which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked. Passages relied on: a customer-managed VPC is required for Private Service Connect and lets several workspaces share one network while reducing the permissions Databricks needs; back-end PSC uses Databricks-specific VPC endpoints so traffic between classic compute and the control plane avoids the public internet, and a front-end option exists but is not in the template; customer-managed keys cover managed services (notebooks, secrets and Databricks SQL query data in the control plane) and workspace storage (the two workspace storage buckets and the GCE persistent disks of compute); private DNS zones are required for back-end PSC so internal names resolve to the endpoints' private addresses.
sources.caveat: Reference templates on a moving main branch, not product documentation; the file was read at the SHA-256 recorded here and may change.

sources.title: Databricks Security Reference Architecture templates: Google Cloud workspace module (psc.tf, vpc.tf, workspace.tf)
sources.reviewedEvidence: psc.tf (SHA-256 530948d9...), vpc.tf (918ac3a2...), workspace.tf (3786894a...) and variables.tf read in full on 2026-09-23 from the main branch through raw URLs, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked. Passages relied on: two internal addresses and two forwarding rules in the customer VPC target the relay and workspace service attachments and are registered as Databricks VPC endpoints for the relay and the REST API; a private Cloud DNS zone for gcp.databricks.com, visible to the workspace VPC, holds A records for the workspace URL, its dp- prefixed variant and tunnel.<region>.gcp.databricks.com, which cluster VMs use to establish the secure tunnel back to the control plane; no Cloud Router or Cloud NAT is created when PSC is used; serverless workspaces set compute_mode and skip the project container and network configuration; storage CMEK applies to classic workspaces only and managed-services CMEK to both; the workspace depends on an ingress firewall rule for the Databricks subnet, and hardened egress without PSC needs the region's control-plane IP addresses.
sources.caveat: Template code on the main branch; its names, defaults and hardening choices are the template's, not requirements, and the firewall rule definitions it depends on were not readable.

sources.title: Compute Engine API v1 discovery document (revision 20260910)
sources.reviewedEvidence: Fetched on 2026-09-23 from the URL above, which this build can reach although docs.cloud.google.com and the Databricks documentation host are blocked; revision 20260910; only the schema descriptions named here were read. Passages relied on: privateIpGoogleAccess says whether VMs in a subnet can access Google services without assigned external IP addresses; a router NAT enables VMs in specified subnetworks to access the internet without external IP addresses; with no access configs an instance has no external internet access; firewall rules allow or deny ingress or egress, direction defaults to INGRESS, priority 0 to 65535 defaults to 1000, lower values take precedence, DENY beats ALLOW at equal priority, and implied rules have priority 65535; rules without target tags or service accounts apply to all instances in the network; a PSC forwarding rule to a managed service targets a service attachment, and pscConnectionStatus is ACCEPTED, PENDING, REJECTED, CLOSED or NEEDS_ATTENTION, PENDING meaning pending acceptance by the producer; a service attachment's consumer accept lists name allowed consumer projects or networks; one service account per VM, its tokens read through the metadata server; organization and network firewall policies are separate resources.
sources.caveat: Machine-readable API reference: field descriptions, not the conceptual guides on docs.cloud.google.com, which this build cannot reach.

sources.title: Cloud Resource Manager API v3 discovery document (revision 20260909)
sources.reviewedEvidence: Fetched on 2026-09-23 from the URL above, which this build can reach although docs.cloud.google.com and the Databricks documentation host are blocked; revision 20260909; schema and method descriptions read. Passages relied on: the organization is the root node of the resource hierarchy to which an entity's resources belong; a folder organizes an organization's resources; a project is a container for ACLs, APIs, VMs and other resources, and its parent is an organization or a folder; setIamPolicy on a project replaces the existing policy, and removing service accounts from policies or changing their roles can make services inoperable.
sources.caveat: API descriptions only; the hierarchy guides on docs.cloud.google.com were not reachable.

sources.title: Organization Policy API v2 discovery document (revision 20260917)

sources.reviewedEvidence: Fetched on 2026-09-23 from the URL above, which this build can reach although docs.cloud.google.com and the Databricks documentation host are blocked; revision 20260903; the ServicePerimeter description read. sources.title: LLM and Agent Evaluation
sources.reviewedEvidence: URL not fetched in this build session (mlflow.org is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy, and the build session's web-search allowance was exhausted before this module was written, so the title and URL were not confirmed by search in this session); it is the evaluation link that the mlflow 3.16.1 README on PyPI and the 3.16.1 UI bundle both use. Page source read on 2026-09-23 from the MLflow repository file docs/docs/genai/eval-monitor/index.mdx at tag v3.16.1, fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com (title 'LLM and Agent Evaluation'). Passage relied on: each evaluation is defined by a dataset (inputs and expectations, optionally pre-generated outputs and traces), scorers (evaluation criteria) and a predict function, run with mlflow.genai.evaluate(); the page lists dataset management, human feedback, LLM-as-a-judge, systematic evaluation and production monitoring.
sources.caveat: The 'latest' documentation moves with each release; the content relied on was read at tag v3.16.1. Vendor phrases about popularity or trust are not repeated.

sources.title: LLM Tracing and Agent Observability
sources.reviewedEvidence: URL not fetched in this build session (mlflow.org blocked by the sandbox egress proxy; search allowance exhausted); it is the link the mlflow 3.16.1 UI labels 'MLflow Tracing documentation' and the README labels 'observability'. Page source read on 2026-09-23 from docs/docs/genai/tracing/index.mdx at tag v3.16.1 via raw.githubusercontent.com. Passage relied on: MLflow Tracing is OpenTelemetry-compatible and captures the inputs, outputs and metadata of each intermediate step of a request; feedback is attached to traces; production monitoring captures latency and token usage per step; production traces can seed evaluation datasets.
sources.caveat: Describes open-source MLflow Tracing; managed Databricks behaviour may differ. Figures about downloads or package size on the page are vendor statements and are not used.

sources.title: LLM Judges and Scorers
sources.reviewedEvidence: URL not fetched in this build session (mlflow.org blocked; search allowance exhausted); it is the 'learn more' link of the scorers pages in the MLflow 3.16.1 web UI bundled inside the installed package. Page source read on 2026-09-23 from docs/docs/genai/eval-monitor/scorers/index.mdx at tag v3.16.1 via raw.githubusercontent.com. Passage relied on: LLM judges and code-based scorers are both scorers in the API; a judge parses the trace, assesses it and returns Feedback attached to the trace; approaches run from built-in judges through Guidelines and custom judges to code-based scorers; the recommended workflow runs from traces through human feedback and error analysis to judges; LLM-as-a-judge has natural biases, so judges should be aligned with human feedback.
sources.caveat: The page calls its built-in judges research-validated; that is the publisher's description, not an independent finding, and this module does not rely on it.

sources.title: Create custom code-based scorers
sources.reviewedEvidence: URL not fetched in this build session (mlflow.org blocked; search allowance exhausted); it is the link the custom code scorer form uses in the MLflow 3.16.1 web UI bundled inside the installed package. Page source read on 2026-09-23 from docs/docs/genai/eval-monitor/scorers/custom/index.mdx at tag v3.16.1 via raw.githubusercontent.com. Passage relied on: the @scorer decorator defines a scorer that may receive inputs, outputs, expectations and the full trace and may return 'yes' or 'no', a bool, a number, a Feedback or a list of Feedback; custom code-based scorers work with mlflow.genai.evaluate() for offline evaluation and are not supported for automatic evaluation; a contains_citation example checks only whether '[source]' appears in the output.
sources.caveat: The page's one-line examples illustrate return types; they are not recommended gates.

sources.title: Building Agent & LLM Evaluation Datasets
sources.reviewedEvidence: URL not fetched in this build session (mlflow.org blocked; search allowance exhausted); it is linked from the MLflow 3.16.1 web UI bundled inside the installed package. Page source read on 2026-09-23 from docs/docs/genai/datasets/index.mdx at tag v3.16.1 via raw.githubusercontent.com. Passage relied on: an evaluation dataset is a selected set of example inputs, labelled with ground-truth expectations or unlabelled, used to test fixes, prevent regressions with a golden set and compare app versions; evaluation datasets require an MLflow tracking server with a SQL backend and are not available with the local file store.
sources.caveat: Requirements for dataset storage differ between open-source MLflow and managed Databricks; check the target platform.

sources.title: Built-in LLM Judges
sources.reviewedEvidence: Fetched on 2026-09-23 (HTTP 200) and read. This is the source of the documentation page that other MLflow pages link as /genai/eval-monitor/scorers/llm-judge/predefined; the rendered mlflow.org page was not fetched. Passage relied on: a table of built-in judges with what each evaluates and whether it needs ground truth or a trace: RelevanceToQuery (neither), Correctness (expected facts), Guidelines and ExpectationsGuidelines, RetrievalRelevance and RetrievalGroundedness (trace required), RetrievalSufficiency (trace and ground truth), ToolCallCorrectness and ToolCallEfficiency (trace required, marked experimental); a note that Safety and RetrievalRelevance are currently only available in Databricks managed MLflow.
sources.caveat: Judge availability changes between releases; the note that some judges are Databricks-managed only was true of the v3.16.1 documentation and must be rechecked.

sources.title: Spans
sources.reviewedEvidence: Fetched on 2026-09-23 (HTTP 200) and read; source of the page other MLflow pages link as /genai/concepts/span; the rendered page was not fetched. Passage relied on: a span records one step of a trace with span_id, trace_id, parent_id (None for the root), name, start and end times, status (OK, UNSET or ERROR), inputs, outputs, attributes and events, compatible with the OpenTelemetry span; predefined span types include CHAT_MODEL, CHAIN, AGENT, TOOL, EMBEDDING, RETRIEVER, PARSER, RERANKER, MEMORY and UNKNOWN; a RETRIEVER span's output is a list of documents with page_content and metadata such as doc_uri and chunk_id; spans can be searched by type.
sources.caveat: Describes the data model; what a real span contains depends on instrumentation.

sources.title: Feedback Concepts
sources.reviewedEvidence: Fetched on 2026-09-23 (HTTP 200) and read; source of the page linked as /genai/concepts/feedback; the rendered page was not fetched. Passage relied on: Feedback records the result of a quality assessment with name, value, rationale, source (HUMAN, LLM_JUDGE or CODE), an optional error and metadata, attached to a trace or to one span in it; LLM judge feedback from evaluation is attached to traces alongside manual checks; revisions and multiple annotators are tracked.
sources.caveat: Describes the assessment record; who may add feedback and where it is stored depend on the deployment.

sources.title: Automatic Evaluation
sources.reviewedEvidence: Fetched on 2026-09-23 (HTTP 200) and read; source of the page linked as /genai/eval-monitor/automatic-evaluations/; the rendered page was not fetched. Passage relied on: automatic evaluation runs LLM judges on traces and multi-turn conversations as they are logged, for quality iteration and production monitoring; it is set up with register() and start() and a ScorerSamplingConfig sample_rate and optional filter string; only LLM judges are supported, not code-based scorers; a newly created or enabled judge evaluates traces at most one hour old; updating a judge's configuration does not re-evaluate traces already assessed; judges run through an AI Gateway endpoint.
sources.caveat: Open-source behaviour at v3.16.1; managed Databricks monitoring may differ, and judge calls cost money: check current pricing before setting a sample rate.

sources.title: Judge Alignment: Teaching AI to Match Human Preferences
sources.reviewedEvidence: Fetched on 2026-09-23 (HTTP 200) and read; source of the page linked as /genai/eval-monitor/scorers/llm-judge/alignment; the rendered page was not fetched. Passage relied on: alignment refines an LLM judge from human feedback; each trace must carry both the judge's assessment and human feedback under the same assessment name as the judge, in either order; the aligned judge is compared with the baseline on held-out data; alignment is repeated as standards change.
sources.caveat: The page quotes an error-reduction range for aligned judges; that is a vendor statement without a published method here, and this module does not repeat it.

sources.title: mlflow 3.16.1
sources.reviewedEvidence: The PyPI project page returned HTTP 200 and the release's project JSON was fetched on 2026-09-23. The same release was installed in this build's ML lab environment and inspected by import: mlflow.genai.evaluate(data, scorers, predict_fn=None, model_id=None); mlflow.genai.scorers exports the built-in judges named in this module, the scorer decorator and ScorerSamplingConfig (sample_rate, filter_string); SpanType includes RETRIEVER, LLM, TOOL, AGENT and GUARDRAIL; AssessmentSourceType includes HUMAN, LLM_JUDGE and CODE; Judge.align(traces, optimizer) exists and the optimizer module failed to import without the DSPy library; the docstrings of get_review_app and create_labeling_session state that the review app and labeling sessions are only available in Databricks.
sources.caveat: An installed package shows which names exist and what their docstrings say; it does not show managed-service behaviour.

sources.title: Judging LLM-as-a-judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
sources.reviewedEvidence: The arXiv page was not fetched (host blocked by the sandbox egress proxy) and the build session's web-search allowance was exhausted before this module was written, so the title and URL were not confirmed by search in this session. The authors' repository README (fastchat/llm_judge/README.md, fetched 2026-09-23 from raw.githubusercontent.com) links this arXiv page and gives the title, authors and 2023 citation; their judge code (fastchat/llm_judge/common.py, fetched the same day) runs each pairwise judgment twice with the two answers swapped and records a disagreeing pair as 'inconsistent'. Passage relied on, as previously read: the paper reports position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases and limited reasoning when LLMs judge chat answers, and proposes mitigations such as swapping positions and reference-guided grading.
sources.caveat: Findings concern the judges and benchmarks studied in 2023; bias strength differs by judge model, rubric and task, so measure your own judge.

sources.title: Databricks SDK for Python v0.141.0: service/iam.py (identity and access APIs)
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the tagged raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; its SHA-256 matches the same file inside the databricks-sdk 0.141.0 wheel published on PyPI that day. Passages relied on: service principals are identities for jobs, automated tools, scripts, apps and CI/CD platforms, and Databricks recommends running production jobs with them so interactive users need no write, delete or modify privileges in production; it is best practice to assign workspace access and Unity Catalog access-control policies to groups instead of individual users, all account identities can be group members, and members inherit their group's permissions; Databricks recommends SCIM provisioning from the identity provider, and terminating a user there removes the user from the Databricks account; with identity federation enabled, user attributes are updated through the account SCIM APIs, not the workspace SCIM APIs; the current-user call returns the authenticated user or service principal; workspace permissions for account principals are ADMIN or USER; job permissions control who can view, manage, trigger, cancel or own a job.
sources.caveat: Docstrings are generated from the API specification and describe API behaviour, not entitlements, tiers or regional availability; setup steps belong to the product documentation.

sources.title: Databricks SDK for Python v0.141.0: credentials_provider.py (authentication strategies)
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the tagged raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; its SHA-256 matches the same file inside the databricks-sdk 0.141.0 wheel published on PyPI that day. The companion files oauth.py and oidc.py at the same tag were also read in full and matched the wheel. Passages relied on: the oauth-m2m strategy needs host, client_id and client_secret, discovers endpoints at /oidc/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server, requests a token with grant_type client_credentials from /oidc/v1/token and adds the refreshed bearer token to every request; tokens are refreshed 40 seconds before expiry; scopes default to all-apis, and offline_access only controls whether a refresh token is issued; the external-browser strategy defaults to the databricks-cli client ID, runs an authorization-code flow with a PKCE S256 challenge and a redirect to http://localhost:8020, and caches tokens under ~/.config/databricks-sdk-py/oauth; the pat strategy needs host and token; OIDC federation exchanges a workload's JWT with the token-exchange grant, authenticating as a service principal when a client ID is given, and uses no rotatable secret; token and client_secret are marked sensitive and print as *** in the configuration debug string.
sources.caveat: Client behaviour of one SDK version; the CLI, Terraform and drivers implement the same flows separately, and token lifetimes are decided by the server, not by this code.

sources.title: Databricks SDK for Python v0.141.0: service/oauth2.py (service principal secrets and federation policies)
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the tagged raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; its SHA-256 matches the same file inside the databricks-sdk 0.141.0 wheel published on PyPI that day. Passages relied on: administrators manage service principal secrets, and a generated secret is used to obtain OAuth access tokens for account and workspace APIs; workspace-level secret APIs need the service principal to be added to the workspace first; account federation policies let users and service principals exchange tokens from a trusted identity provider for Databricks OAuth tokens, remove the need to manage Databricks secrets, and are typically combined with SCIM; service principal federation (workload identity federation) lets workloads outside Databricks authenticate as a service principal with tokens from their runtime and no Databricks secret; Databricks strongly recommends it over OAuth client secrets or personal access tokens whenever possible; it is supported by services including GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, GitLab, Terraform Cloud and Kubernetes; a policy specifies the accepted issuer and the permitted subject.
sources.caveat: API docstrings, not a configuration guide; which identity providers a given account trusts is decided by its own policies.

sources.title: Databricks SDK for Python v0.141.0: service/workspace.py (Secrets API)
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the tagged raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; its SHA-256 matches the same file inside the databricks-sdk 0.141.0 wheel published on PyPI that day. Passages relied on: administrators, secret creators and users granted permission can read Databricks secrets, and while Databricks makes an effort to redact secret values displayed in notebooks, it is not possible to prevent such users from reading them; an ACL names a user or group and one of MANAGE (change ACLs, read and write), WRITE (read and write) or READ (read and list); secret values can in general be read only from within a command on a cluster, with the permission of whoever runs the command, who needs at least READ; changing an ACL requires MANAGE, and the API throws PERMISSION_DENIED when the caller lacks permission.
sources.caveat: Describes the Databricks-backed secret API; cloud-specific backends and newer secret objects are outside this record.

sources.title: Databricks SDK for Python v0.141.0: service/jobs.py (job run-as settings)
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the tagged raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; its SHA-256 matches the same file inside the databricks-sdk 0.141.0 wheel published on PyPI that day. Passages relied on: the run-as setting specifies the user, service principal or group a job runs as, and if it is not specified the job runs as the user who created it; a service principal is named by its application ID, and setting it requires the servicePrincipal/user role; run_as_user_name defaults to the job's creator when job access control is disabled or to the user with the is_owner permission when it is enabled.
sources.caveat: The SDK also lists a group run-as option whose availability was not verified here; this record is used only for user and service principal run-as behaviour.

sources.title: Databricks SDK for Python v0.141.0: service/catalog.py (row filters, column masks, ABAC policies, system schemas)
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the tagged raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; its SHA-256 matches the same file inside the databricks-sdk 0.141.0 wheel published on PyPI that day. Passages relied on: a table row filter names the full name of a SQL UDF and the table columns passed to it, whose types must match the function's arguments; a column mask names a SQL UDF whose first argument has the masked column's type, with optional additional columns; ABAC policies control access based on data attributes rather than specific resources, support conditions on securable properties, governance tags and environment contexts, require the MANAGE privilege on the securable to view, create, update or delete them, and a new policy applies to the securable and all its descendants; a system schema lives in the system catalog and may contain usage information such as audit logs, billing logs and lineage.
sources.caveat: API field descriptions; supported compute, runtimes and access paths for filters, masks and policies are documented elsewhere and change.

sources.title: Databricks SDK for Python v0.141.0: service/settings.py (tokens and token management)
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the tagged raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; its SHA-256 matches the same file inside the databricks-sdk 0.141.0 wheel published on PyPI that day. Passages relied on: the Token API creates, lists and revokes tokens used to authenticate to Databricks REST APIs; token management lets administrators get all tokens and delete tokens for other users, including all tokens of one user; an on-behalf-of token for a service principal takes a lifetime in seconds; a token record carries its creator, owner, creation time, expiry time, comment and an approximate last-used day accurate to one day.
sources.caveat: API behaviour only; whether token creation is allowed at all is a workspace setting and permission.

sources.title: Databricks Terraform provider v1.133.0: provider documentation (authentication)
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the provider's v1.133.0 tag (release dated 2026-09-21 in the provider changelog) through its raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; the same file on the main branch was compared and matched. Passages relied on: Databricks strongly recommends OAuth instead of personal access tokens for user account client authentication and authorization; client_id is the service principal's application ID and client_secret its secret, usable at account and workspace level on all supported clouds; after databricks auth login, tools can reuse the cached OAuth token of that CLI profile; workload identity federation authenticates automated workflows with tokens issued by the automation environment; accepted auth types include pat, oauth-m2m, databricks-cli, github-oidc, env-oidc and file-oidc.
sources.caveat: Provider documentation, not the product documentation site; the linked product pages hold the setup steps.

sources.title: Databricks Terraform provider v1.133.0: databricks_service_principal resource
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the provider's v1.133.0 tag (release dated 2026-09-21 in the provider changelog) through its raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; the same file on the main branch was compared and matched. The group and mws_permission_assignment pages at the same tag were read with it. Passages relied on: a Databricks-managed service principal exists only inside the Databricks platform on all clouds and cannot access non-Databricks services, while an Azure-managed service principal is an existing Azure identity registered in Databricks; account-level service principals are assigned to workspaces with a workspace permission assignment, and workspace entitlements are set separately; the group resource manages both account groups and workspace-local groups, and group members can be users, service principals and other groups; an account-level principal is assigned to a workspace with USER or ADMIN permission.
sources.caveat: Provider documentation; entitlement names and deletion behaviour are provider-level details to recheck before automation.

sources.title: Databricks Terraform provider v1.133.0: databricks_secret resource
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the provider's v1.133.0 tag (release dated 2026-09-21 in the provider changelog) through its raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; the same file on the main branch was compared and matched. The secret_scope and secret_acl pages at the same tag were read with it. Passages relied on: writing a secret requires WRITE or MANAGE on the scope; a secret key is at most 128 characters, a value at most 128 KB, and a scope holds at most 1000 secrets; a secret value can be read only from within a command on a cluster, with the invoker's permission, which must be at least READ; a secret can be referenced as {{secrets/scope/key}} in Spark configuration and environment variables; the scope creator receives MANAGE unless the initial manage principal is users; an ACL principal may be a user name, a group display name (users meaning all workspace users) or a service principal application ID, with READ, WRITE or MANAGE.
sources.caveat: Limits quoted here are the provider page's statements and should be rechecked against the current Secrets API before design.

sources.title: Databricks Terraform provider v1.133.0: databricks_service_principal_secret resource
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the provider's v1.133.0 tag (release dated 2026-09-21 in the provider changelog) through its raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; the same file on the main branch was compared and matched. Passages relied on: the resource creates a secret for a service principal that can be used to request OAuth tokens for the Databricks REST APIs; without a lifetime the secret has a default lifetime of 730 days (63072000s); exported attributes include the sensitive secret, create_time, expire_time and status such as ACTIVE; a time_rotating dependency forces recreation for rotation.
sources.caveat: The default lifetime is the provider page's statement at this release; confirm the current default before relying on it.

sources.title: Databricks Terraform provider v1.133.0: databricks_obo_token resource
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the provider's v1.133.0 tag (release dated 2026-09-21 in the provider changelog) through its raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; the same file on the main branch was compared and matched. The databricks_token page at the same tag was read with it. Passages relied on: on-behalf-of tokens are created for a service principal in workspaces on AWS and Google Cloud, and it is generally best to use OAuth with a client ID and secret and to keep these tokens for integrations that do not support OAuth; permission to use tokens is granted as CAN_USE on the tokens authorization object, and declaring it overwrites token-usage permissions of existing groups such as users unless they are included; personal access tokens are created for the authenticated user with a lifetime in seconds and can be rotated by recreation.
sources.caveat: On-behalf-of tokens are documented for AWS and Google Cloud workspaces; Azure uses native OAuth flows.

sources.title: Databricks Terraform provider v1.133.0: databricks_service_principal_federation_policy resource
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the provider's v1.133.0 tag (release dated 2026-09-21 in the provider changelog) through its raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; the same file on the main branch was compared and matched. The account_federation_policy page at the same tag was read with it; both carry a GA release-stage badge. Passages relied on: service principal federation policies let automated workloads outside Databricks access Databricks APIs without Databricks secrets, authenticating as a service principal with tokens issued by the workload runtime such as GitHub Actions; a policy names the identity provider (issuer) and the workload identity (subject) allowed to authenticate as the service principal; audiences, from the token's aud claim, default to the Databricks account ID; the subject claim defaults to sub; Databricks recommends discovering signing keys from the issuer's well-known endpoint; account federation policies let users and service principals use tokens from trusted identity providers and are typically used with SCIM.
sources.caveat: The GA badge describes the provider resource's release stage at v1.133.0; issuer and subject formats belong to each workload platform.

sources.title: Databricks Terraform provider v1.133.0: databricks_policy_info resource (ABAC policies)
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the provider's v1.133.0 tag (release dated 2026-09-21 in the provider changelog) through its raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; the same file on the main branch was compared and matched. The page carries a GA release-stage badge. Passages relied on: ABAC policies control access based on data attributes rather than specific resources; they support conditions on governance tags and the user identity; callers need MANAGE on a securable to view, create, update or delete them; supported actions include applying a row filter or a column mask to a table; the scope is a catalog, a schema or a table; to_principals and except_principals name user or group names the policy applies to or excludes; match_columns selects table columns by condition such as hasTag('pii'); a column mask function's first argument and return type should match the masked column; the API also lists grant and deny policy types.
sources.caveat: The page's GA badge describes the provider resource at v1.133.0; the product documentation's status label, supported compute and regional availability were not read in this build and must be checked.

sources.title: Databricks Terraform provider v1.133.0: databricks_access_control_rule_set resource
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the provider's v1.133.0 tag (release dated 2026-09-21 in the provider changelog) through its raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; the same file on the main branch was compared and matched. The tag_policy page at the same tag was read with it. Passages relied on: rule sets grant roles on account-level resources; on a service principal, roles/servicePrincipal.manager manages the principal and roles/servicePrincipal.user allows using it; on a group, roles/group.manager manages it; account rule sets include tag policy creator, manager and assigner roles, and tag policies define the governed tags of the account; the resource is authoritative and overwrites existing permissions of the same type.
sources.caveat: Authoritative per object in Terraform: declaring it overwrites existing rules of the same type.

sources.title: Databricks Terraform provider v1.133.0: databricks_system_schema resource
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the provider's v1.133.0 tag (release dated 2026-09-21 in the provider changelog) through its raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; the same file on the main branch was compared and matched. Passages relied on: system tables are a Databricks-hosted analytical store of the account's operational data for historical observability; system tables must be enabled by an account admin; the example enables the access schema; the resource identifier combines the metastore ID and schema name, and the full name has the form system.<schema>.
sources.caveat: Some schemas are enabled automatically and some cannot be disabled; enablement state is per metastore.

sources.title: dbt-databricks v1.12.5: row filter and column mask SQL macros
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the v1.12.5 release tag (release dated 2026-09-01 in the adapter changelog) through its raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; column_mask.sql and the row_filters and column_masks functional tests at the same tag were read with it, and the macros matched the main branch. Passages relied on: a row filter is attached with ALTER TABLE <table> SET ROW FILTER <catalog.schema.function> ON (<columns>) or WITH ROW FILTER in CREATE, and removed with DROP ROW FILTER; a column mask is attached with ALTER TABLE <table> ALTER COLUMN <column> SET MASK <function> USING COLUMNS (<other columns>) and removed with DROP MASK; the tests create a filter as a SQL function RETURNS BOOLEAN over a column, create a mask as a SQL function RETURNS STRING, and assert that a plain SELECT returns the masked value; filters and masks are listed in information_schema.row_filters and system.information_schema.column_masks; neither works on the Hive metastore.
sources.caveat: Adapter code, not the SQL language reference; clause options beyond those the adapter emits are not covered here.

sources.title: Databricks Terraform provider v1.133.0: databricks_mws_log_delivery resource (audit log delivery)
sources.reviewedEvidence: File read in full on 2026-09-23 from the provider's v1.133.0 tag (release dated 2026-09-21 in the provider changelog) through its raw URL, which this build can reach although the documentation host is blocked; the same file on the main branch was compared and matched. Passages relied on: audit logs are delivered as JSON files with a static schema to a path of the form delivery-prefix/workspaceId=<id>/date=<yyyy-mm-dd>/auditlogs_<id>.json; logs are available within 15 minutes of activation, new files arrive every few minutes, data sometimes arrives later than 15 minutes, and delivered files may be overwritten with additional lines for more events to give exactly-once semantics; a delivery configuration cannot be deleted, only disabled.

sources.title: 3.4. Transactions

sources.title: 13.2. Transaction Isolation
sources.reviewedEvidence: Search-result title and snippet confirmed 2026-09-23; page body not fetched in this build (documentation host blocked by the sandbox egress proxy). Passage relied on, as previously read: Read Committed is the default: each statement sees data committed before the statement began. Repeatable Read sees only data committed before the transaction's first statement and prevents all phenomena except serialization anomalies; a Repeatable Read transaction that tries to update a row changed by a concurrent committed transaction is rolled back with could not serialize access due to concurrent update; Serializable emulates serial execution; applications using these levels must be prepared to retry transactions that fail with serialization failures.
sources.caveat: Describes PostgreSQL itself; a managed service built on Postgres can add limits, which its own documentation states.

sources.title: 13.3. Explicit Locking
sources.reviewedEvidence: Search-result title and snippet confirmed 2026-09-23; page body not fetched in this build (documentation host blocked by the sandbox egress proxy). Passage relied on, as previously read: FOR UPDATE locks the rows retrieved as though for update, preventing other transactions from locking, modifying or deleting them until the current transaction ends; row-level locks do not affect data querying and block only writers and lockers of the same row; locks are held until the end of the transaction; deadlocks can arise from row-level locks, and PostgreSQL detects them and resolves them by aborting one of the transactions.
sources.caveat: Covers lock modes in general; the SELECT reference owns the exact locking-clause syntax.

sources.title: SELECT
sources.reviewedEvidence: Search-result title and snippet confirmed 2026-09-23; page body not fetched in this build (documentation host blocked by the sandbox egress proxy). Passage relied on, as previously read: The locking clause locks the returned rows until the end of the transaction; with NOWAIT the statement reports an error rather than waiting if a selected row cannot be locked immediately; with SKIP LOCKED any selected rows that cannot be immediately locked are skipped, which gives an inconsistent view of the data unsuitable for general work but usable to avoid lock contention with multiple consumers of a queue-like table.
sources.caveat: Locking behaviour interacts with ORDER BY and LIMIT as the page describes; test queue queries under concurrency.

sources.title: INSERT
sources.reviewedEvidence: Search-result title and snippet confirmed 2026-09-23; page body not fetched in this build (documentation host blocked by the sandbox egress proxy). Passage relied on, as previously read: ON CONFLICT specifies an alternative action to raising a unique or exclusion constraint violation: DO NOTHING skips the row, DO UPDATE updates the existing row and guarantees an atomic insert-or-update outcome even under high concurrency; the proposed row is available as EXCLUDED; DO UPDATE requires a conflict target and accepts a WHERE condition; RETURNING returns rows actually inserted or updated.
sources.caveat: ON CONFLICT needs a unique index or constraint that matches its conflict target; other errors still abort the statement.

sources.title: Serverless compute plane networking

sources.title: High-level architecture

sources.title: What is OpenSharing?

sources.title: Lineage in Unity Catalog

sources.title: Row filters and column masks
sources.reviewedEvidence: Column masks are query-time functions returning original or masked column values; row filters restrict returned rows. Supported access paths and runtimes have explicit limits.
sources.caveat: Table-level masks differ from ABAC policies and dynamic views. They are query visibility controls, not proof of encryption or universal protection of every external path.

sources.title: Machine learning on Databricks

sources.caveat: Platform capabilities do not establish a valid target, enough representative labels or useful customer outcomes.

sources.title: Common pitfalls and recommended practices

sources.caveat: scikit-learn 1.9.1 documentation reviewed 2026-09-20; principles are general ML reasoning, not a Databricks execution.

sources.title: Cross-validation: evaluating estimator performance
sources.reviewedEvidence: Holdout discussion separates fitting, tuning and final evaluation; time-dependent and grouped data require split strategies reflecting those dependencies.

sources.title: Metrics and scoring: quantifying prediction quality
sources.reviewedEvidence: Binary classification section defines confusion-matrix counts, precision TP/(TP+FP), recall TP/(TP+FN) and threshold-dependent measures.

sources.title: Tuning the decision threshold for class prediction
sources.reviewedEvidence: Decision-threshold discussion separates score estimation from the action threshold and warns against fitting/tuning on the same data.
sources.caveat: A probability threshold is an operational choice; default 0.5 is not a universal business optimum.

sources.title: ML Experiment Tracking

sources.title: Data profiling

sources.title: Probability calibration: calibration curves
sources.reviewedEvidence: Calibration curves compare a bin’s mean predicted probability with its observed positive fraction; bin sample counts matter.
sources.caveat: A small observed bin is uncertain; calibration evidence is population-dependent and is not causal benefit.

sources.title: precision_score
sources.reviewedEvidence: Precision is true positives divided by true plus false positives.
sources.caveat: The prevalence experiment is original synthetic arithmetic holding recall and false-positive rate fixed; real population changes need fresh evidence.

sources.title: recall_score: averaging and support
sources.reviewedEvidence: Macro averaging weights class recalls equally; weighted averaging weights each class by its true sample count, called support.
sources.caveat: A chosen averaging rule does not encode every operational consequence; report class-level counts too.

sources.title: MLflow Model Registry: versions and aliases
sources.reviewedEvidence: A registered model contains numbered versions; a model alias is a mutable named reference to a particular version.

sources.title: ML Experiment Tracking

sources.reviewedEvidence: Read in this build on 2026-09-23 from the downloaded wheel (SHA-256 matched PyPI; uploaded 2026-09-23), files databricks/sdk/service/aisearch.py and aifunctions.py. AiSearchAPI is described as an 'AIP-conformant replacement for the legacy VectorSearchEndpoints API; functionally equivalent'. IndexType DELTA_SYNC 'automatically syncs with a source Delta Table, automatically and incrementally updating the index'; DIRECT_ACCESS 'supports direct read and write of vectors and metadata through our REST and SDK APIs'. PipelineType TRIGGERED 'stops after refreshing the source table once, using the data available when the update started'; CONTINUOUS 'processes new data as it arrives'. sources.title: Delta Sharing Protocol
sources.reviewedEvidence: Read in this build on 2026-09-23 from the raw file (raw.githubusercontent.com, HTTP 200; SHA-256 ff2631fb8177fb8acd9cc448db3c5179e1df6e0e0cf5b933904a39ffd457535c): the Overview, Concepts, Access Modes, Query Table Version, Read Data from a Table (request body and File), Read Change Data Feed, Generate Temporary Table Credential, Capabilities Header and Profile File Format sections. Passage relied on: a share groups schemas and tables for recipients and a table is a Delta table or a view on one; a recipient is a principal holding a bearer token, and every REST API uses bearer tokens; Read Data from a Table returns files as HTTPS URLs the client reads directly, with an optional expirationTimestamp, or, with directory-based access, temporary read-only credentials with an expirationTime; predicateHints, jsonPredicateHints and limitHint are best effort and the client must apply them itself; version and timestamp reads need history sharing; a client may cache file content by file id and use Query Table Version to detect a stale cache; the delta response format enables reading tables with minReaderVersion above 1, such as those with deletion vectors or column mapping, and a client that did not request it must fail if the server answers in it; the profile file holds shareCredentialsVersion, endpoint, bearerToken and an optional expirationTime whose absence means the token can be seen as never expiring.
sources.caveat: A specification states what servers and clients may do; a given server, including Databricks', may implement optional fields such as URL expiration timestamps differently. Pin a commit when citing exact behaviour.
