Passage relied on, read in the protocol schema definitions shipped in mcp-types 2.2.0: tools are listed with tools/list and invoked with tools/call over JSON-RPC 2.0; a Tool has a name, a description that can be thought of as a hint to the model, an inputSchema that is a JSON Schema object with type object at its root, and an optional outputSchema; every ToolAnnotations property (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint) is a hint not guaranteed to describe the tool faithfully, with defaults false, true, false and true, and clients should never make tool use decisions based on annotations received from untrusted servers; errors that originate in a tool are reported inside CallToolResult with isError set to true so the model can see them, while errors in finding the tool are protocol errors.
sources.caveat: A protocol specification describes messages and expected client and server behaviour; it enforces nothing in any implementation. Revisions are dated, so check which one a client and server use.

sources.title: urllib3 2.6.3: Retry
sources.reviewedEvidence: Installed package source read locally in this build on 2026-09-23. Passage relied on: Retry's allowed_methods defaults to the methods considered idempotent (multiple requests with the same parameters end with the same state), DELETE, GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT and TRACE, so POST is not retried by default, and None retries any verb; between attempts after the second try it sleeps backoff_factor times 2 to the power of previous retries, optionally plus jitter, never longer than backoff_max, and backoff is disabled by default.
sources.caveat: One client library's defaults; other clients differ, and no client setting makes a server operation idempotent.

sources.title: Data warehouse system architecture
sources.reviewedEvidence: Search-result title and snippet confirmed 2026-09-23; page body not fetched in this build (the documentation host is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy (HTTP 403 at CONNECT on 2026-09-23)). Snippet: the listing title is 'Data warehouse system architecture - Amazon Redshift'; the leader node manages communication with client programs and compute nodes, parses and develops execution plans, compiles code and distributes it to the compute nodes, which run it and return intermediate results for final aggregation; a compute node is partitioned into slices, each allocated a portion of the node's memory and disk space. The page's Markdown source, doc_source/c_high_level_system_architecture.md in the awsdocs/amazon-redshift-developer-guide repository (master branch), from which this URL is generated, was read on 2026-09-23 through raw.githubusercontent.com. AWS's repository README says the repository was archived in June 2023 and that its content is out of date. Passage relied on, from that source: a cluster is one or more compute nodes, and with two or more a leader node parses queries, develops execution plans and distributes compiled code to the compute nodes; compute nodes are divided into slices, and a table's distribution key decides how its rows are distributed to the slices; Redshift Managed Storage keeps warehouse data in a separate tier that scales on Amazon S3, so compute and storage are sized and paid for independently; Amazon Redshift is based on PostgreSQL, with a number of very important differences that designers must take into account.
sources.caveat: Details from the archived source, marked out of date by AWS since June 2023; node types and storage options may have changed. The live page's snippet agrees on leader node, compute nodes and slices.

sources.title: Database security
sources.reviewedEvidence: Search-result title and snippet confirmed 2026-09-23; page body not fetched in this build (the documentation host is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy (HTTP 403 at CONNECT on 2026-09-23)). Snippet: the listing title is 'Database security - Amazon Redshift' (localized listings of the same page still carry 'Managing database security'); database security is managed by controlling which users have access to which database objects; role-based access control assigns permissions to roles applied to users, and unlike groups, roles can inherit permissions from other roles; row-level security policies restrict access to chosen rows and are applied to users or groups; dynamic data masking transforms data at query runtime. The page's Markdown source, doc_source/r_Database_objects.md in the awsdocs/amazon-redshift-developer-guide repository (master branch), from which this URL is generated, was read on 2026-09-23 through raw.githubusercontent.com. AWS's repository README says the repository was archived in June 2023 and that its content is out of date. Passage relied on, from that source: by default permissions are granted only to the object owner; users receive permissions directly or by membership of a group; schemas collect tables and other objects and cannot be nested; role-based access control assigns permissions to roles that are applied to users, and unlike groups, roles can inherit permissions from other roles; row-level security policies restrict the rows users or groups can access; dynamic data masking transforms sensitive data at query runtime.
sources.caveat: Details from the archived source, marked out of date by AWS since June 2023, whose title was 'Managing database security'; the live listing agrees on roles, inheritance, row-level security and masking. Check the live pages for the policy options a real estate uses.

sources.title: Snowflake key concepts and architecture

sources.caveat: Only the search snippet was read in this build; the three-layer detail is as previously read and must be re-checked against the current page before an assessment relies on it.

sources.title: HDFS Architecture
sources.reviewedEvidence: Search-result title and snippet confirmed 2026-09-23; page body not fetched in this build (the documentation host is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy (HTTP 403 at CONNECT on 2026-09-23)). Snippet: the listing title is 'Apache Hadoop 3.3.5 – HDFS Architecture' at this stable URL; HDFS has a master/slave architecture with a single NameNode that manages the file system namespace and regulates client access, and DataNodes that manage storage on their nodes; a file is split into blocks stored on DataNodes; user data never flows through the NameNode. The page's Markdown source, hadoop-hdfs-project/hadoop-hdfs/src/site/markdown/HdfsDesign.md in the apache/hadoop repository (trunk branch), from which this URL is generated, was read on 2026-09-23 through raw.githubusercontent.com. Passage relied on, from that source: an HDFS cluster has a single NameNode that manages the file system namespace and DataNodes that store blocks; files are write-once except for appends and truncates and have strictly one writer at any time; HDFS is designed more for batch processing than interactive use, emphasising throughput over latency; moving computation is assumed cheaper than moving data, and HDFS offers interfaces for applications to move themselves closer to where the data is located.
sources.caveat: Read from the trunk branch source, which can be newer than the stable release this URL serves (the listing names 3.3.5).

sources.title: HDFS Permissions Guide
sources.reviewedEvidence: Search-result title and snippet confirmed 2026-09-23; page body not fetched in this build (the documentation host is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy (HTTP 403 at CONNECT on 2026-09-23)). Snippet: the listing title is 'Apache Hadoop 3.3.5 – HDFS Permissions Guide' at this stable URL; the model shares much of the POSIX model, each file and directory having an owner and a group with separate permissions for the owner, group members and all others; a check tests owner, then group, then other permissions; optional POSIX ACLs add rules for named users and groups. The page's Markdown source, hadoop-hdfs-project/hadoop-hdfs/src/site/markdown/HdfsPermissionsGuide.md in the apache/hadoop repository (trunk branch), from which this URL is generated, was read on 2026-09-23 through raw.githubusercontent.com. Passage relied on, from that source: HDFS implements a permissions model for files and directories that shares much of the POSIX model: each file and directory has an owner and a group, with separate permissions for the owner, group members and all other users, and optional POSIX ACLs add rules for named users and groups; a client's identity comes from the host operating system in simple mode or from Kerberos credentials, and the identity mechanism is extrinsic to HDFS.
sources.caveat: Read from the trunk branch source (the listing names 3.3.5). Deployment-specific policy layers on a real cluster are outside this page.

sources.title: Migration Guide: SQL, Datasets and DataFrame
sources.reviewedEvidence: Search-result title and snippet confirmed 2026-09-23; page body not fetched in this build (the documentation host is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy (HTTP 403 at CONNECT on 2026-09-23)). Snippet: listing titles for the 4.0.0, 4.0.2 and latest pages were shown; the results returned no passage text. The page's Markdown source, docs/sql-migration-guide.md in the apache/spark repository (tag v4.0.4), from which this URL is generated, was read on 2026-09-23 through raw.githubusercontent.com. The 4.0.4 rendered path did not surface in search, so the record cites the 4.0.2 page of the same 4.0 line, whose listing title is 'Migration Guide: SQL, Datasets and DataFrame - Spark 4.0.2 Documentation'; the sections relied on describe 4.0 and 3.0 changes present in every 4.0.x guide. Passage relied on, from that source: since Spark 4.0 spark.sql.ansi.enabled is on by default, and CREATE TABLE without USING or STORED AS uses spark.sql.sources.default instead of Hive as the provider; since Spark 4.0 the legacy datetime rebasing configurations lose their spark.sql.legacy prefix; in Spark 3.0 the Proleptic Gregorian calendar replaced the hybrid Julian and Gregorian calendar used by Spark 2.4 and below, changing results for dates before 15 October 1582; in Spark 3.0 table insertion follows ANSI store assignment, so an out-of-range value raises a runtime exception where Spark 2.4 inserted the low-order bits (257 inserted into a byte column became 1); Spark SQL is designed to be compatible with the Hive Metastore, SerDes and UDFs and supports the vast majority of Hive features.
sources.caveat: Open-source Spark behaviour; a vendor runtime can set different defaults, so confirm the setting in force on the target compute.

sources.title: ANSI Compliance
sources.reviewedEvidence: Search-result title and snippet confirmed 2026-09-23; page body not fetched in this build (the documentation host is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy (HTTP 403 at CONNECT on 2026-09-23)). Snippet: the listing title is 'ANSI Compliance - Spark 4.0.2 Documentation'; there are two options to comply with the SQL standard, spark.sql.ansi.enabled and spark.sql.storeAssignmentPolicy; by default spark.sql.ansi.enabled is true and Spark SQL uses an ANSI-compliant dialect instead of being Hive compliant; Spark throws an exception at runtime instead of returning null results when the inputs to an operator or function are invalid. The page's Markdown source, docs/sql-ref-ansi-compliance.md in the apache/spark repository (tag v4.0.4), from which this URL is generated, was read on 2026-09-23 through raw.githubusercontent.com. The 4.0.4 rendered path did not surface in search, so the record cites the 4.0.2 page of the same 4.0 line. Passage relied on, from that source: by default spark.sql.ansi.enabled is true and Spark SQL uses an ANSI-compliant dialect instead of being Hive compliant, so Spark throws an exception at runtime instead of returning null results when the inputs to an operator or function are invalid; spark.sql.storeAssignmentPolicy defaults to ANSI; try_divide is identical to the division operator except that it returns NULL instead of throwing an exception on dividing by 0.
sources.caveat: Engine defaults differ across products and versions; check the setting in force before relying on either behaviour.

sources.title: Spark SQL, Built-in Functions
sources.reviewedEvidence: Search-result title 'Spark SQL, Built-in Functions' confirmed 2026-09-23 at the latest-documentation path (a 4.0.x path did not surface); page body not fetched in this build (the documentation host is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy (HTTP 403 at CONNECT on 2026-09-23)). Snippet: the div operator divides expr1 by expr2, returns NULL if an operand is NULL or expr2 is 0, and casts the result to long. The reference is generated from the usage text of each expression; the Divide and IntegralDivide usage text in sql/catalyst/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/catalyst/expressions/arithmetic.scala at the apache/spark tag v4.0.4 was read on 2026-09-23 through raw.githubusercontent.com. Passage relied on: the / operator returns expr1/expr2 and always performs floating point division, with SELECT 3 / 2 returning 1.5; div divides expr1 by expr2 and casts the result to long, with SELECT 3 div 2 returning 1.
sources.caveat: The generated page itself was not fetched; its usage text describes a NULL result for a zero divisor under div while the ANSI page says invalid inputs raise under the default ANSI mode, so confirm the behaviour on the target runtime rather than from either text.

sources.title: ORDER BY Clause
sources.reviewedEvidence: Search-result title and snippet confirmed 2026-09-23; page body not fetched in this build (the documentation host is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy (HTTP 403 at CONNECT on 2026-09-23)). Snippet: the listing title is 'ORDER BY Clause - Spark 4.2.0 Documentation' at the latest path; if null_sort_order is not specified, NULLs sort first for ascending order and last for descending order, and NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST return NULL values first or last regardless of the sort order. The page's Markdown source, docs/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-orderby.md in the apache/spark repository (tag v4.0.4), from which this URL is generated, was read on 2026-09-23 through raw.githubusercontent.com. A 4.0.x rendered path did not surface in search, so the record cites the latest page; the listing showed the same null-ordering rule for releases from 3.2 to 4.2. Passage relied on, from that source: if the null sort order is not specified, NULLs sort first when the sort order is ASC and last when it is DESC; NULLS FIRST and NULLS LAST return NULL values first or last regardless of the sort order.
sources.caveat: Open-source Spark syntax reference; confirm behaviour on the target engine's own reference.
